key_terms.meaning: The association of a name with an object such as a storage location, a type or a value; it can happen at language-design, compile, link, load or run time.
The mapping from names to storage locations that is active at a point in the program; the state is the separate mapping from locations to values.
A use of a name refers to the declaration found by searching the enclosing blocks of the program text, outermost search following the source nesting.
A use of a name refers to the declaration in the most recently entered still-active procedure at run time, so the answer depends on the call chain, not the text.
Code segment (fixed size) + static/global area (fixed size) + stack (grows one way) + heap (grows the other way).
The part of execution between the moment storage is allocated for it and the moment that storage is released; lifetime decides the region.
Storage placed at a fixed address decided before execution, so the name keeps one address for the whole run; no recursion allowed.
Storage pushed on the run-time stack when a procedure is entered and popped when it returns; matches the last-in-first-out order of calls.
Storage taken from a free pool at any time and released at any time, so data can outlive the procedure that created it.
The block of stack memory holding one call of a procedure: return value, actual parameters, control link, access link, saved machine status, locals and temporaries.
A field in an activation record pointing to the record of the caller, used when the callee returns.
A field pointing to the activation record of the statically enclosing procedure, used to reach non-local names; its size in hops is the nesting depth difference.
FP marks the base of the current activation record, SP marks the current top of the stack; locals sit at fixed offsets from FP.
The caller evaluates the argument and copies its value into the callee's frame, so the callee cannot change the caller's variable.
The caller passes the address of the argument; the callee works directly on the caller's storage, so changes are visible after return.
Copy in at call, copy back out at return; the callee is isolated during execution but the final value reaches the caller.
The text of the argument is substituted for the formal parameter and re-evaluated at each use, implemented with a thunk.
Lazy variant of call by name: the argument's thunk is evaluated at most once, and the stored value is reused on later uses.
A data structure mapping each name to its attributes (type, kind, scope, offset, size) so the compiler can answer lookups in near-constant time.
The process, done during semantic analysis, of deciding which declaration a given use of a name refers to by searching symbol tables from innermost scope outward.

takeaways: The compiler can only place a name correctly once it knows which activation of which procedure the name belongs to; scope and binding rules give that answer.
Run-time memory is carved into code, static, stack and heap regions, and each datum goes to the region that matches its lifetime.
Static allocation is fast but forbids recursion; stack allocation follows calls naturally; heap allocation is the only one that lets data outlive its creator.
One call of a procedure equals one activation record, and the caller and callee split the work of building, filling and destroying it.
The control link restores the caller on return; the access link lets a nested procedure reach the variables of its enclosing procedure.
The parameter passing mechanism decides whether the callee sees a copy or the original storage, and that single decision can change the printed output.
Call by value is safe but costs a copy; call by reference is cheap but creates aliases; call by value-result and call by name exist for special needs.
The symbol table plus scope rules are what turn a name in the source into a specific storage offset in a specific frame.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit usually ask you to draw the run-time memory picture and the activation records for a given program, then justify each field and each storage choice, so practise diagramming nested calls and parameter passing side by side.

bank.q: Explain the three storage allocation strategies — static, stack and heap — stating the lifetime rule each obeys and the restriction each imposes on the source language.
outline: Static: addresses fixed before run time, no recursion, no dynamic arrays
Stack: push on entry, pop on return, LIFO matches call order
Heap: allocate and free at arbitrary times, needed for data outliving its procedure
Table comparing allocation time, deallocation, cost of access, restrictions
Example showing recursion failing under static allocation

bank.q: Draw and explain the fields of an activation record and state which fields the caller fills and which the callee fills.
outline: Return value, actual parameters, control link, access link, saved machine status, local data, temporaries
Caller evaluates and pushes arguments, saves return address, jumps
Callee saves registers and old FP, sets FP, allocates locals, returns result
Epilogue restores SP, FP and registers
Diagram of two stacked records

bank.q: Define binding time and list the binding times for a variable's name, storage, type and value with one example each.
outline: Language design time: meaning of keywords and operators
Implementation time: size of int
Compile time: offsets of locals
Link and load time: addresses of external globals
Run time: values, heap objects, actual parameters

bank.q: Describe how a symbol table stores entries and compare linear list, sorted list and hash table organisations for insert and lookup.
outline: Attributes stored: name, kind, type, scope, offset, size, line
Linear list: O(n) lookup, simple
Sorted list: O(log n) with binary search, costly insert
Hash table with chaining: average O(1) both operations
Scope handling with a stack of tables or a scope field

bank.q: Explain call by value, call by reference, call by value-result and call by name, and show with one small program how their outputs differ.
outline: Mechanism of each, with what is copied or shared
Aliasing under call by reference
Copy-in copy-out order effects under value-result
Thunk and re-evaluation under call by name, Jensen's device
Trace of the same program under each mechanism

bank.q: For a program with procedures P calling Q calling R, where R refers to a variable declared in P, draw the stack of activation records and show how the access link chain resolves the reference.
outline: Draw three frames with control links and access links
Access link of R points to frame of P (difference 2)
Number of hops equals nesting depth difference
Alternative: display array indexed by depth
Effect of the reference being one level up instead

bank.q: A recursive function is called to depth 4 while a global array and two heap objects exist. Draw the run-time memory map, mark the four frames, and compute the stack size if each frame is 64 bytes.
outline: Code, static, stack and heap regions with growth directions
Four frames stacked, control links downward
Locals at negative offsets from FP
Stack use = 4 × 64 = 256 bytes plus saved registers
Pointer to heap object stored in a local

bank.q: Given declarations of a procedure, compute the size of its activation record and the offset of each local, assuming 4-byte integers and 8-byte alignment for the record.
outline: List fields with sizes
Round each field to its alignment
Pad the record to a multiple of 8
Offset of each local from FP
Why outgoing argument space is reserved by the caller

bank.q: Write the sequence of stack and frame pointer changes for a call and a return, starting from the caller's code and ending back in it.
outline: Caller pushes arguments, saves return address
Callee pushes old FP, sets FP = SP
Callee decrements SP for locals, saves registers
On return SP = FP, pop old FP, pop return address
Caller adjusts SP to remove arguments

bank.q: A procedure nests three levels deep inside enclosing procedures. Explain how a non-local reference is compiled using (a) access links and (b) a display array, and compute the hops needed.
outline: Static link points to the record of the textually enclosing procedure
Hops = current depth − target depth
Following the chain at run time
Display is an array of frame pointers indexed by depth
Cost comparison: chain is O(d), display is O(1)

bank.q: Analyse why call by name is difficult to implement and what goes wrong when the argument expression has side effects. Compare it with call by need.
outline: Argument passed as a thunk, evaluated at every use
Repeated evaluation cost and repeated side effects
Aliasing and write-through behaviour
Call by need evaluates once and caches, so cost falls but evaluation order is fixed
Example of a side-effecting expression giving different results

bank.q: Compare static and dynamic scoping for a program with nested and non-nested procedures. Evaluate how each affects the compiler's symbol table and the run-time access cost.
outline: Static scope resolved at compile time, offsets fixed
Dynamic scope needs deep access or shallow access at run time
Shallow access keeps a save stack per name
Deep access searches the control link chain
Effect on readability, separate compilation and speed

bank.q: Evaluate stack versus heap allocation for objects whose lifetime is not known at compile time, and explain how closures force escape of local variables to the heap.
outline: Stack fits strict LIFO lifetimes only
Escaping data must move to the heap
Closure keeps captured environment alive after return
Cost of heap: slower allocation, garbage collection
Escape analysis to keep some objects on the stack

bank.q: For passing a large array of 10⁶ integers to a procedure, evaluate call by value against call by reference and call by value-result, in terms of copy cost, aliasing and safety.
outline: Call by value copies 4 MB per call (10⁶ × 4 bytes)
Call by reference passes one address, but callee can modify caller's data
Value-result copies in and out, doubling copy cost but blocking aliasing during the call
Aliasing hazards when two formals refer to the same array
Practical recommendation and the const qualifier

glossary.def: One execution of a procedure, from the call to the return, with its own copy of local data.
The stack block holding the parameters, links, saved state, locals and temporaries of one activation.
The moment at which a name is associated with a meaning, a type or a storage location.
Parameter passing in which the argument text replaces each use of the formal and is re-evaluated every time.
Call by name in which the thunk is evaluated once and its value cached for later uses.
Parameter passing in which the address of the argument is given to the callee.
Parameter passing in which no value goes in but the callee's final value is copied back to the caller's argument.
Parameter passing in which a copy of the argument's value is placed in the callee's frame.
Copy in at call and copy back at return, combining isolation during the call with an output value.
The instructions split between caller and callee that build and destroy an activation record.
A procedure together with the environment in which it was created, so its free names stay reachable.
Pointer in an activation record to the caller's record, used to restore state on return.
Pointer in an activation record to the record of the textually enclosing procedure.
An array of frame pointers indexed by nesting depth, giving constant-time access to non-local names.
Another name for the control link.
The mapping from names in force at a program point to storage locations.
Register holding the base address of the current activation record, so locals sit at fixed offsets from it.
The memory region from which storage is allocated and freed at arbitrary times.
The interval between allocation and release of a datum's storage.
The region of program text in which a declaration of a name is visible.
Another name for the access link.
The compiler's table mapping each name to its attributes such as type, kind, scope and offset.
A small piece of code plus its environment that computes an argument's value on demand, used for call by name.
Two or more names that refer to the same storage location.
